David Copperfield. Serialized from 1849 to 1850, this novel is Charles Dickens's most autobiographical work. It's a bildungsroman narrated by the adult David Copperfield, looking back on his life from birth through adulthood. The novel opens with his birth and the mistreatment that follows his father's death. Two figures rescue him: Peggotty, his faithful nurse, and her brother Dan Peggotty, who becomes a father figure to the boy. As David grows, he encounters Uriah Heep, his great rival and the novel's central villain. Heep is a hypocritical and obsequious clerk whose false humility masks ruthless ambition and duplicity. Against Heep stands Agnes Wickfield, the gentle and deeply moral heroine who will become David's ultimate love and his wife. She represents his emotional grounding and his path to stability. There is also Steerforth, David's charismatic friend whose personal magnetism blinds David to his moral rot. When Steerforth seduces Little Em'ly, Dan Peggotty's daughter, it brings tragedy to everyone involved, though it ultimately leads to redemption. Dickens drew heavily on his own childhood trauma for this novel, particularly his experience of childhood abandonment, making it his most introspective and personally revealing work of all his major novels. The novel traces not just David's physical journey but his emotional and moral development as he learns who he truly is.
